slides.0.title: Routes to market and market structure
slides.0.subtitle: To sell, wine first has to reach the consumer
slides.1.title: Basic types of channel
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Off-trade (retail)
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Supermarkets, specialist shops and online retail; supermarkets sell in volume with fierce price competition, while specialists offer selection and advice and are better at selling small regions and premium wine
slides.1.highlights.1.title: On-trade (hospitality)
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Restaurants, bars and hotels; smaller volumes but strong for brand image, and sommelier recommendations are often the entry point for new regions
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Importers and distributors
slides.1.highlights.2.content: They handle customs, storage, logistics and sales teams; for small wineries, finding the right importer often matters more than trade fairs
slides.1.content: Different channels need different wines: volume retail wants price, the on-trade wants a story, specialists want distinctiveness.
slides.2.title: Regulated markets
slides.2.highlights.0.title: State monopolies
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Sweden’s Systembolaget and Canadian provinces (e.g. Ontario’s LCBO, Québec’s SAQ) run government retail monopolies; they buy by tender, in large volumes and to strict specifications, and are key customers for many wineries
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The US three-tier system
slides.2.highlights.1.content: After Prohibition most states required producers, wholesalers and retailers to be separate; the 2005 Granholm v. Heald ruling barred states from discriminating against out-of-state wineries on direct shipping, opening interstate DTC, but the three-tier system itself remains lawful
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Tariffs and trade agreements
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Tariffs can change a market overnight: from 2020 China imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties of up to about 218% on Australian wine, exports to China collapsed, and the duties were lifted only in March 2024; conversely, the Japan–Chile EPA helped Chile become Japan’s top supplier by volume in 2015
slides.2.content: Policy risk belongs in every export essay: tariffs, monopolies and distribution laws can rewrite a market.
slides.3.title: Direct sales and special trading systems
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Direct to consumer (DTC)
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Cellar door, wine clubs, online shops and wine tourism; cutting out intermediate mark-ups gives high margins and direct customer data, making it a key channel for small and mid-sized wineries
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Bordeaux’s La Place
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Châteaux sell through brokers (courtiers) to many négociants, who sell worldwide; en primeur sales happen before bottling, giving châteaux early cash while buyers bet on future appreciation
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Co-operatives and négociants
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Co-operatives pool small growers’ grapes and provide scale, equipment and market access; négociants buy grapes or wine and sell under their own brands (Champagne NM, Burgundy négociants); both let small vineyards reach international markets
slides.3.content: Channel choice decides who keeps the margin: the closer to the consumer, the higher the margin but the smaller the scale.
